nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the sensation novel and the domestic serial
literary_identity: Novelist; the author of East Lynne, the most successful sensation novel of the 1860s and one of the most performed plays of the century.
biography: Born Ellen Price at Worcester on 17 January 1814, the daughter of a glove manufacturer; she married Henry Wood in 1836 and lived in France before returning to England in 1856. East Lynne (1861) made her famous and was reprinted eight times in its first year; she edited the Argosy from 1867 and wrote over thirty novels. She died in London on 10 February 1887.
literary_profile: Mrs Henry Wood wrote the Victorian domestic sensation novel with a moral seriousness that her rivals lacked: East Lynne is the story of a wife who elopes, loses her child, returns as a governess and dies of remorse, and its combination of adultery, retribution and maternal grief made it the century's most successful example of the form. Her novels are the finest record of the Victorian middle-class home under threat.
stylistic_characteristics: Direct, urgent narrative address; the domestic interior rendered in detail; the moral catastrophe that follows a single error; the deathbed scene; the author's commentary and warning; the serial cliff-hanger.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage, adultery and the fallen woman; the family and its destruction; class, inheritance and legitimate birth; mothers and children; the law and the courtship plot; the middle-class home and its secrets.
historical_significance: Mrs Henry Wood is the most successful woman novelist of the sensation school and East Lynne one of the central novels of the 1860s: it sold in hundreds of thousands, was dramatised all over the world for fifty years, and its portrait of the erring wife and the lost child made it the definitive Victorian sensation novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the comic opera, the burlesque and the comic verse
literary_identity: Dramatist and librettist; the author of the Savoy operas and one of the greatest comic writers in English.
biography: Born William Schwenck Gilbert in London on 18 November 1836; he served as a militia officer, was called to the bar in 1864, and made his name with the Bab Ballads (1869) and the burlesques. His collaboration with Arthur Sullivan began with Thespis in 1871 and produced fourteen operas, from Trial by Jury (1875) to The Gondoliers (1889), staged by Richard D'Oyly Carte at the Savoy. He was knighted in 1907 and died at Grim's Dyke, Harrow, on 29 May 1911.
literary_profile: Gilbert wrote the English comic opera, and in doing so he wrote the English comic tradition of the late century: his librettos unite the topsy-turveydom of the burlesque with a satire of the professional and legal classes, and their verbal dexterity — the patter song, the logical absurdity, the inverted proverb — is unmatched. His early Bab Ballads are the finest comic verse of the period after Lear, and his stagecraft made the Savoy opera the most successful theatrical enterprise of the age.
stylistic_characteristics: Inverted logic carried to absurdity; the patter song with accelerating syllable count; rhyming of impossible words; satire of the law, the army, the peerage and the aesthetic movement; the chorus of the conventional and the individual who defies it; comic verse with illustrations.
intellectual_concerns: The law, the state and the professions; class and the peerage; aestheticism and the 'greenery-yallery' pose; love, marriage and the war of the sexes; duty, duty and the parody of duty; the Englishman abroad and the satire of national character.
historical_significance: Gilbert is the greatest English librettist and one of the greatest comic writers in the language: the Savoy operas are the most successful theatrical works ever produced in Britain, they created a permanent repertory and a national comic idiom, and the Bab Ballads are a classic of English nonsense verse.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the well-made play, the problem drama and the social comedy
literary_identity: Dramatist; the master of the well-made play and the writer who brought the moral problem of the 1890s onto the English stage.
biography: Born Arthur Wing Pinero in London on 24 May 1855, the son of a solicitor; he trained as an actor and joined the Lyceum company in 1876, then turned to playwriting, producing a long series of farces and comedies in the 1880s. The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893) made him the most discussed dramatist in England; he wrote The Notorious Mrs Ebbsmith, Trelawny of the 'Wells', The Gay Lord Quex and Mid-Channel, and was knighted in 1909. He died in London on 23 November 1934.
literary_profile: Pinero made the English stage serious: his farces gave the 1880s their comic idiom, and his problem plays of the 1890s — above all The Second Mrs Tanqueray — put the fallen woman, the double standard and the woman with a past at the centre of a drama built with the mechanical perfection of the well-made play. He was the professional playwright as craftsman, and his stagecraft was the technical foundation on which Shaw and Wilde built.
stylistic_characteristics: The well-made play: the expository first act, the crisis, the scène à faire and the inevitable conclusion; dialogue of London society with its clipped idiom; stage directions of meticulous precision; the problem stated and then followed to its social consequence; a comic subplot counterpointing the serious action.
intellectual_concerns: The woman with a past and the double standard; marriage, divorce and respectability; the theatre and its professional world; class, money and the marriage market; the New Woman and the claims of the individual; the provincial town and the London stage.
historical_significance: Pinero is the greatest English craftsman of the well-made play and the dramatist who made the Victorian stage confront the moral questions of the 1890s: The Second Mrs Tanqueray is the central English problem play before Shaw, Trelawny of the 'Wells' is a permanent classic of the theatrical comedy, and his technical example shaped the modern English theatre.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the melodrama, the problem play and the drama of the provinces
literary_identity: Dramatist; the most prolific serious playwright of the 1880s-90s and one of the first English dramatists to argue for a national theatre.
biography: Born Henry Arthur Jones at Grandborough, Buckinghamshire, on 20 September 1851, the son of a farmer; he left school at twelve and worked as a draper's assistant and a commercial traveller before writing his first play in 1878. The Silver King (1882), with Henry Herman, made him rich; Saints and Sinners (1884), The Middleman (1889) and Mrs Dane's Defence (1900) established him as a serious dramatist. He campaigned for a national theatre and died in London on 7 January 1929.
literary_profile: Jones wrote the English melodrama and then the English problem play: The Silver King is the finest melodrama of the 1880s, and his later work — The Middleman, Mrs Dane's Defence, The Liars — treats industrial conflict, the double standard and the moral cowardice of society with a seriousness that prepared the way for Shaw. He was also the most articulate English advocate of a national theatre and a professional dramatic literature.
stylistic_characteristics: The strong melodramatic situation with a moral core; the social problem dramatised through a family; dialogue of the manufacturing middle class; the cross-examination scene; the direct address to the audience on a question of the day.
intellectual_concerns: The double standard and the fallen woman; industrial capital and the middleman; religious hypocrisy and the Nonconformist conscience; class and the social ladder; marriage and respectability; the provinces and the metropolis.
historical_significance: Jones is the central English dramatist of the transition from melodrama to the problem play: The Silver King was the most successful melodrama of its decade, Mrs Dane's Defence is one of the finest English problem plays before Shaw, and his campaign for a national theatre made him the most important theatrical publicist of the period.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the hospital poem, the imperial ode and the editor's magazine
literary_identity: Poet, critic and editor; the author of 'Invictus' and the most influential literary editor of the 1890s.
biography: Born William Ernest Henley in Gloucester on 23 August 1849, the son of a bookseller; tuberculosis of the bone led to the amputation of his leg in 1873-75 at the Edinburgh Infirmary, where he wrote the poems of In Hospital. He edited the Magazine of Art, the Scots Observer and the National Observer, discovered Kipling and was a friend of Stevenson, who modelled Long John Silver on him. He died in Woking on 11 July 1903.
literary_profile: Henley wrote the English poetry of endurance and of the imperial idea: 'Invictus' became one of the most quoted poems in the language, and the hospital poems of In Hospital are the first English poems to treat a patient's experience with clinical realism. As an editor he shaped the literature of the 1890s more than any other single figure, and his magazine published the early work of Kipling, Yeats and Wells.
stylistic_characteristics: Short, hard, rhymed verse in the ballad and the song measure; the hospital poem of exact physical detail; the imperial ode with its rhetorical refrain; the critical essay that discovers and defines a new writer; the editorial anthology of the new movement.
intellectual_concerns: Illness, surgery and the body; courage, endurance and the unconquerable will; the sea, the hospital and the city; empire, the English race and the imperial destiny; friendship and the literary life; the new poetry of the 1890s.
historical_significance: Henley is the central English literary editor of the 1890s and the author of 'Invictus', one of the most quoted poems in the language: his National Observer was the nursery of the literature of the decade, In Hospital is a landmark of English poetry about illness, and his influence on Kipling, Yeats and the whole 'new poetry' was decisive.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the classical lyric, the metrical experiment and the poet laureate
literary_identity: Poet and physician; the Poet Laureate from 1913 and the finest English technical poet of his generation.
biography: Born Robert Seymour Bridges at Walmer, Kent, on 23 October 1844; he studied medicine at Oxford, where he met Gerard Manley Hopkins, and practised at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London until 1882, when he retired to Yattendon, Berkshire, to write. He published The Growth of Love (1876), Shorter Poems (1890) and The Testament of Beauty (1929); he edited Hopkins's poems in 1918 and was Poet Laureate from 1913. He died at Boar's Hill, Oxford, on 21 April 1930.
literary_profile: Bridges wrote the classical English lyric with a perfection of technique unmatched in his generation except by Housman: his short poems of love, nature and mortality are models of form, and his long metrical experiments — the sonnet sequence, the quantitative hexameters, the 'loose Alexandrines' of The Testament of Beauty — make him the most technically inventive English poet of his age. He is also the editor who made Hopkins known to the world.
stylistic_characteristics: Exquisite metrical control in received forms; classical smoothness and restraint; a private, unfashionable lyric quietness; experiment in quantitative and accentual metre; the long philosophical poem in a new metre; the poem of English landscape and rural peace.
intellectual_concerns: Love, beauty and the passing of the seasons; mortality and the consolations of nature; the English countryside and rural peace; religion and the modern world; the art of poetry itself; time and the permanence of beauty.
historical_significance: Bridges is the finest English technical poet of his generation and the editor who preserved Hopkins for the language: The Testament of Beauty was a best-seller in 1929 and made him a public figure, his lyrics are models of form, and his edition of Hopkins changed the course of English poetry.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the imperial ballad and the poetry of the public school
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and historian; the author of 'Vitaï Lampada' and the laureate of the Victorian public school and the imperial idea.
biography: Born Henry John Newbolt at Bilston, Staffordshire, on 6 June 1862, the son of a vicar; he was educated at Clifton College and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, was called to the bar in 1887, and published Admirals All in 1897. His ballads of the navy and the public school made him the most popular poet of the imperial movement; he edited the Nelson classics and wrote the official history of the naval operations of the First World War. He was knighted in 1915 and died in London on 19 April 1938.
literary_profile: Newbolt wrote the poetry of the imperial ideal: 'Vitaï Lampada' is the most famous English poem about the playing fields of the public school as the training ground of empire, and his naval ballads gave the late-Victorian navy its literary image. He is also the key witness to the English ideal of the gentleman-sportsman, and his poems are the essential documents of the imperial imagination at its most confident.
stylistic_characteristics: Ballad measure with a strong refrain; the schoolboy and the naval anecdote; the moral drawn from a game; the cadenced appeal to duty and tradition; the rhetoric of the imperial mission; the plain, memorable lines.
intellectual_concerns: The public school and the making of the English gentleman; duty, discipline and the imperial mission; the navy and the sea; sport, cricket and the ethos of fair play; the empire and the English race; the Great War and its commemoration.
historical_significance: Newbolt is the central poet of the English imperial ideal and the public school: 'Vitaï Lampada' is one of the most quoted and most parodied English poems, his naval ballads shaped the image of the navy, and his work is the indispensable document of the imperial imagination of the 1890s.

alternative_names: George Louis Palmella Busson du Maurier
nationality_or_literary_tradition: French-born British; the comic illustration, the society novel and the psychological romance
literary_identity: Illustrator and novelist; the author of Trilby, the most popular novel of the 1890s, and the creator of Svengali.
biography: Born George Louis Palmella Busson du Maurier in Paris on 6 March 1834; he studied chemistry and then art, lost the sight of one eye, and settled in London in 1860, where he became the principal illustrator of Punch for thirty years. His social cartoons created the Victorian image of the aesthetic and the nouveau riche; Trilby (1894) sold in enormous numbers and gave the world Svengali. He died in London on 8 October 1896.
literary_profile: Du Maurier's Trilby is the great popular novel of the 1890s and one of the founding texts of modern mass culture: its story of the tone-deaf model hypnotised into a great singer by the sinister Svengali gave the language a word and a myth, and its bohemian Paris made the art student a permanent figure of the popular imagination. His Punch drawings are the definitive visual record of Victorian middle-class manners.
stylistic_characteristics: Direct, confiding narration with comic digression; the bohemian studio and the Latin Quarter; the sinister hypnotist as villain; sentiment and the supernatural; comic illustrations integrated with the text; the society party and the fashionable salon.
intellectual_concerns: Bohemia and the artist's life; hypnotism and the manipulation of the will; love, beauty and the artist's model; the Englishman abroad and the Latin Quarter; class, manners and the nouveaux riches; the power of the manipulator.
historical_significance: Du Maurier is the central Victorian comic illustrator and the author of Trilby, one of the most popular novels of the century: it created Svengali and the idea of the hypnotic manipulator, it made bohemian Paris a popular literary subject, and his Punch drawings are the essential visual record of Victorian middle-class life.
